messages.author: 3e3ca0351e8e43f2
messages.subject: Variance from detection probability
parts:
Dear All,



I have surveyed large mammals on transects in Cambodia from 2006 to 2010.
The data for most species behave fairly normally at reasonable sample sizes,
but wild pigs are presenting problems. For 2009 and 2010 I am analysing each
year separately as we have sufficient observations. Analysis shows that p of
chi-squared is up to 0.9, however coefficient of variation of the group and
individual densities is up to 60%. Detection probability also explains over
80% of individual density variance, but encounter rate and cluster size show
explain less than 10% each. This is somewhat unusual as most other species
have a higher proportion of variance explained by encounter rate. Other
species found in large groups do not show high variance from detection
probability.



Notes

1. There are a relatively large number of observations at a distance
of 0 m (27 out of 63 observations in 2009, 26 out of 84 observations in
2010) and I am aware that in 2009 there was a problem with the survey team
estimating distances inaccurately and placing them at convenient distances.

2. Wild pigs can occur in large groups of up to, but most observations
are of singletons, but cluster size.



Does anyone have experience of this problem and can explain this issues?



Thanks in advance.



Hugo



Hugo Rainey, PhD

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Variance from detection probability
parts:
Hugo, this used to be a very common problem, which we see less often
now, both because the message is getting through better that you need
accurate distance estimates and because the technology is better and
cheaper for measuring distances - e.g. laser rangefinders.
Unfortunately, when such a high proportion of detections is recorded as
at zero distance, reliable estimation of the detection function is not
possible. Note that this problem can also occur if transects are along
trails, and the species of interest uses the trails. If you've ruled
out that possibility (solution is to place transects randomly; if you
have to cut transects, do a minimum cut, so as not to create obvious
trails), and are confident that this is a measurement issue, then it can
only be resolved by training of the observers. In your current
analyses, you are likely to be overestimating densities, because you're
trying to fit a spike in the detection function at zero distance which
probably isn't real. That leads you to underestimate the proportion of
animals on the strip that you detect and overestimate abundance. The
same problem is often encountered in primate surveys. Off the list,
I'll send a copy of the following paper, which discusses this issue.

Steve Buckland

Buckland, S.T., Plumptre, A.J., Thomas, L. and Rexstad, E.A. 2010.Design
and analysis of line transect surveys for primates./International
Journal of Primatology/ *31*, 833-847.
